newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serbs agree extension of OSCE mission.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs agree extension of OSCE mission.

text.p: Bosnian Serb authorities have agreed to extend the mission of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to supervise municipal elections in 1997, the OSCE said on Sunday.

"We feel that this is a solid agreement. It is based on an understanding between OSCE and Republika Srpska (Serb republic) which will require close consulations as we proceed over the next several months," said OSCE's Bosnia chief, Robert Frowick.
"My own suggestion is that it would be best to hold them (municipal elections) probably in the latter part of June, but before the second half of 1997."
Frowick said the agreement was struck with Biljana Plavsic, president of Bosnia's Serb republic covering 49 percent of the country.
Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation, comprising the remainder of the country, had already agreed to extend the OSCE mission for the purpose of overseeing local elections.

Serb approval came just two days before an OSCE-sponsored summit on Bosnia in Lisbon at which Frowick, an American, would have been embarrassed to appear without clearance for his mission's proposed 1997 election role.
The Dayton peace agreement, signed one year ago this month, ended the Bosnian war and assigned OSCE the role of supervising the country's first post-war national and municipal voting.
National elections were held on September 14. Allegations of fraud, which the OSCE denied, tainted the electoral process and led to mixed reviews abroad of OSCE stewardship.

Municipal elections were twice postponed as a result of OSCE concerns about voter registration problems. The OSCE has struggled to resolve disputes over how to register several million refugees and displaced persons who are unable to return to their homes.
Frowick acknowledged problems with the September national elections and said lessons learned the last time around would be the basis for tighter procedures in the 1997 municipal vote.

"We needed to work out an approach to refugee voting problems. Throughout the year the most problematic single issue involving rules and regulations was refugee voting," Frowick told reporters in Sarajevo.

"We have created an application procedure. That had never happened before. We will be doing much better on those kinds of issues as well as on the complete registration of the voters both inside the country and abroad."
Dayton provides for refugees living abroad to cast votes in the community in which they resided before the war, or in a community in which they intend to reside upon returning.
Ethnic separatists steered refugee votes into contested areas in the September elections to try to ensure their ethnic group dominated new municipal authorities.

In order to avoid similar abuses in the 1997 municipal elections, the OSCE has tightened the application procedure for those who want to vote in a community other than their pre-war home, Ambassador Frowick said.
